statement: In New York City in 1993 to 1995, days on which that day's or the previous day's highest temperature reached 31.1 °C (88 °F) (146 of 1,095 days, here called hot days), compared with other days, were associated with more deaths certified by the city's medical examiner as unintentional cocaine overdose: 2.34 a day against 1.76 (341 deaths on hot days, 1,667 on other days), a third more (Marzuk et al., 1998); by the editors' calculation a rate ratio of 1.33 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.49), or about 85 deaths more than the other-day rate predicts, some 4 in 100 of the 2,008 cocaine overdose deaths of those three years. The days were compared without any adjustment for season, day of the week, holidays or trend, and nobody's heat exposure, amount used or pattern of use was known. Deaths from opiates with cocaine absent or present only in clinically insignificant amounts were 0.81 against 0.71 a day and other overdose deaths 0.08 on both kinds of day, neither difference significant, but by the editors' calculation the opiate rate ratio (1.14, 0.93 to 1.38) did not differ significantly from the cocaine one (ratio of the two 1.17, 0.93 to 1.47), so the paper's reading that the rise was specific to cocaine is not established; the share of homicide and traffic victims with cocaine in their blood was much the same on hot and other days (18.9 against 19.5 in 100; 9.5 against 10.3 in 100), which the authors read as cocaine use not rising on hot days; and opiates were also found in about 6 in 10 of the deaths counted as cocaine overdoses. The temperature threshold was chosen from the 1990 to 1992 overdose deaths and the dates of heat deaths with cocaine, then tested on the 1993 to 1995 deaths; the heat-death sampling window was 1990 to 1995 and included those test years, so threshold choice was not demonstrated to be wholly independent of the test period; of 40 tested deaths certified as due to overheating (hyperthermia) in 1990 to 1995, 10 had a breakdown product of cocaine in the body. In a laboratory experiment (Crandall et al., 2002), 7 healthy adults aged 23 to 37 who had never used cocaine were heated at rest in a suit carrying water at 46 °C after one intranasal dose of cocaine (2 mg per kg, described by the authors as low; study conditions) and, on another day in random order, after the same dose of lidocaine, a local anaesthetic used as the comparison (called placebo in the abstract): before heating, core temperature did not differ (36.79 against 36.75 °C), but during heating it rose more after cocaine (P < 0.001; to about 37.79 against 37.55 °C after about 38 minutes, read from the paper's figure and approximate); the skin's blood vessels began to widen, and sweating began, at a core temperature about 0.3 °C higher (37.37 against 37.06 °C and 37.38 against 37.07 °C; by the editors' calculation, 95% CIs of about 0.11 to 0.51 and 0.16 to 0.46 °C); at a core temperature of 37.86 °C, forearm skin vascular conductance (blood-flow signal divided by blood pressure) was 49 against 70 in 100 of its site maximum and sweat rate 0.8 against 1.0 mg per cm² per minute (number contributing is not stated; these are the text values, while Figure 2 has differing plotted endpoints and does not identify the contrast behind its significance label); and people felt less hot at the same core temperature. Heat production was not measured, so the authors' conclusion that cocaine raises body temperature mainly by impairing heat loss is an inference; they expect larger doses to add heat production, say the results may not apply to people who use cocaine regularly, and did not test their suggestion that hot weather and crowded clubs amplify the effect. Neither study followed people who used cocaine in hot weather. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In New York City in the 1990s, hot days had about a third more deaths recorded as cocaine overdoses than other days (2.34 against 1.76 a day). The days were compared without allowing for season or anything else that comes with summer, and the study could not show that the rise happened only with cocaine. In a laboratory, 7 healthy people who had never used cocaine were heated after one small dose: their skin began to flush and sweat only at a higher body temperature, their body temperature rose more than after a comparison drug, and they felt less hot. Neither study looked at people using cocaine in hot weather.

risk_of_bias.note: Day comparison (card sc_marzuk_1998): ROBINS-E high, entirely unadjusted (season, day of week, holidays and trend not modelled); deaths counted through the medical examiner's certification; the negative-control comparisons are imprecise and were not compared with the cocaine estimate. Laboratory study (card sc_crandall_2002): RoB 2 some concerns (how the order was randomized not reported; blinding not checked although cocaine raised heart rate and blood pressure, which matters for the felt heat; number contributing at the highest temperatures unknown; no protocol; about 22 comparisons without correction).

inconsistency.note: The two studies answer different parts of the question (deaths on hot days; heat-loss responses in the laboratory), and no replication of either was read.

indirectness.note: One city in 1993 to 1995 and counts of deaths per day, not anyone's own heat exposure or use; the laboratory study gave one low intranasal dose to 7 people who had never used cocaine, heated passively at rest, unlike use outside the laboratory (larger or repeated amounts, exertion, other drugs).

imprecision.note: Seven people in the laboratory, with the intervals for the comparisons at 37.86 °C close to no difference; the opiate comparison cannot exclude a rise of about a third. The cocaine rate ratio itself is precise (1.18 to 1.49).

large_effect.note: Not applied: a rate ratio of 1.33 from an unadjusted comparison.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the paper's 'steady increase' above the threshold rests on cumulative and moving-average curves without a test of trend (card reporting issues).

grade.reasoning: The day comparison is observational and starts low; rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, it is very low. The laboratory study, rated alone, would start high as a randomized crossover and be rated down for risk of bias, indirectness (one low dose in people who had never used cocaine, at rest) and imprecision (7 people), also very low. 'Is associated with': the death counts come from an unadjusted comparison of days, and the laboratory study shows what one dose did to heat-loss responses under passive heating, not what happens to people who use cocaine in hot weather. Status single study: each part rests on one study; the laboratory study is consistent with the death counts but does not replicate them, and it takes them as its starting point. Not read: the editorial on the New York study (Kilbourne, 1998), the published letter on the laboratory study with the authors' reply (Schier et al., 2002), a later study of the same association (Auger et al., 2017) and population studies of heat and drug deaths on the reading list. The post-mortem cocaine levels that the laboratory paper's introduction cites are second-hand and not used.
